macro: The Fed has held its policy rate at 3.50%-3.75% since July, when three regional bank presidents dissented in favor of a hike; minutes released August 19 showed broad hawkish sentiment even as Chair Kevin Warsh floated cutting the annual meeting count from eight to six. Jobless claims fell to 206,000 for the week ended August 15, beating the 210,000 forecast, while Friday's S&P Global flash PMI showed the composite economy holding at 54.1 (beating a 53.5 forecast) even as manufacturing contracted to 48. Geopolitical risk stayed elevated as the US-Iran standoff over the Strait of Hormuz continued, keeping a premium in oil prices. The single most important date to watch this week is Wednesday, August 26, when the July core PCE inflation report and Nvidia's fiscal second-quarter earnings land on the same day.

mortgage_rate: The 30-year fixed mortgage rate averaged 6.65% for the week of August 20, 2026, down from 6.67% the week before, per Freddie Mac's PMMS survey. Rates easing toward their lowest level since spring are giving buyers modest relief even as July existing-home sales fell 1.7% and inventory held near a 4.6-month supply.
personal_finance_deep_dive: The New York Fed's Q2 2026 Household Debt and Credit Report shows student loan balances fell $7 billion to $1.65 trillion, one of only two debt categories to decline, while new serious delinquencies (90+ days past due) dropped to 7.83% from 12.88% a year earlier. The improvement follows the post-restart default wave that pushed delinquency rates sharply higher through 2025, suggesting more borrowers are catching up on payments now that servicers have worked through the backlog. The pattern is uneven across debt categories: credit card and auto balances have kept climbing even as mortgage and student debt shrank, indicating households are prioritizing which obligations to pay down first rather than deleveraging broadly.
wealth_building_deep_dive: A new Investment Company Institute survey finds 47% of 401(k) and similar plan participants say they probably would not save for retirement if they didn't have a plan at work, rising to 58% among those earning under $50,000 a year. The mechanism is structural: automatic payroll deduction and employer matching remove the moment-to-moment decision to save, which is where most manual retirement plans break down. A reader without workplace access to a plan could replicate the effect this week by setting up an automatic weekly or biweekly transfer into an IRA timed to land right after each paycheck, removing that same decision friction.
